\chapter{Reading — Words, Lines, and a First Encounter}
\label{ch:ar-first-reading}
\hlchaptermodality{42}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read familiar Arabic words without romanization, follow complete lines in right-to-left script, and understand a connected encounter from greeting through a choice to farewell.}

One complete Arabic encounter made only from previously taught forms and glyphs, with the script carrying greeting, names, a choice and farewell without a romanized line underneath.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[(reading)]{(reading) — six old words, with the training wheels gone}

\label{lesson:AR-C42-words}



\begin{quote}
You have heard, said and written every word below. Nothing here is new.

What is new is the empty space beneath each word. There is no romanized line to catch you. Let the Arabic carry its own sound.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
\begin{quote}
\ar{سلام} \ar{شكرًا} \ar{شاي} \ar{نعم} \ar{لا} \ar{حسنًا}
\end{quote}

Read down once, right to left, without translating.

Read again. The first and third words stretch an \textbf{\ar{ا}} into a long sound, while \textbf{\ar{شكرًا}} and \textbf{\ar{حسنًا}} share the little \textbf{\ar{ـًا}} ending.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{cousinweb}
Arabic letters change coat when they join, but they do not change identity. The \textbf{\ar{ح}} in \textbf{\ar{حسنًا}} is the same hook body you learned in \textbf{\ar{خير}}; the word only asks you to recognize it at speed.

And \textbf{\ar{لا}} is still the lām-alif pair from chapter five. Reading is not a new script lesson. It is trusting the shapes you already paid for.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the six words in order, once, without stopping
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two words share the written \textbf{\ar{ـًا}} ending? (\textbf{\ar{شكرًا،} \ar{حسنًا}}.)

How many new Arabic words did you meet? (\textbf{None.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(reading)]{(reading) — six lines that already know each other}

\label{lesson:AR-C42-lines}



\begin{quote}
The last lesson gave you words standing alone. Now the words join other words, in the same way that the letters inside them join one another.

You have said every line. Read the Arabic first; let meaning arrive before any romanization does.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
\begin{quote}
\ar{السلام} \ar{عليكم}. \ar{وعليكم} \ar{السلام}. \ar{ما} \ar{اسمك؟} \ar{اسمي} \ar{سامي}. \ar{شاي} \ar{أو} \ar{حليب؟} \ar{شاي}.
\end{quote}

Read all six lines once without stopping.

Read again. The question mark tells you where a voice asks; the full stop tells you where it answers. Arabic puts its question mark the other way round — \textbf{\ar{؟}} — because the line itself runs the other way.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{اسمي} \ar{سامي}} has no written word for \emph{is}. The zero copula from chapter two is not missing ink; it is how an Arabic present-tense sentence works.

That is one gift of reading whole lines: the blank between ideas can carry grammar too. You already learned that blank by ear. Now you can see it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the six lines in order, once, without stopping
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two lines ask questions? (\textbf{\ar{ما} \ar{اسمك؟} \ar{شاي} \ar{أو} \ar{حليب؟}})

Where is \emph{is} in \textbf{\ar{اسمي} \ar{سامي}}? (\textbf{Nowhere on the page — Arabic does not need it here.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(reading)]{(reading) — the first whole encounter}

\label{lesson:AR-C42-first-passage}



\begin{quote}
Six words, then six lines. Now read one encounter from its first peace to its last.

Every form has appeared before. The only new thing is holding all of them together without a romanized line underneath.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
\begin{quote}
\ar{السلام} \ar{عليكم}. \ar{وعليكم} \ar{السلام}. \ar{ما} \ar{اسمك؟} \ar{اسمي} \ar{سامي}. \ar{مرحبًا} \ar{يا} \ar{سامي}. \ar{شاي} \ar{أو} \ar{حليب؟} \ar{حليب؟} \ar{لا}. \ar{شاي؟} \ar{نعم}. \ar{حسنًا}. \ar{شكرًا}. \ar{مع} \ar{السلامة}.
\end{quote}

Read the whole encounter once. Do not stop to translate a word; let each turn answer the turn before it.

Read it again. This time notice the hinge: \textbf{\ar{شاي} \ar{أو} \ar{حليب؟}} One choice becomes two tiny questions, then a clear answer.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{cousinweb}
A connected passage does not have to be one speaker's paragraph. Here the connection is the work each line does: greeting invites reply, a name invites welcome, and \textbf{\ar{شاي} \ar{أو} \ar{حليب؟}} opens a choice.

\textbf{\ar{لا}} closes the first option. \textbf{\ar{نعم}} accepts the second. \textbf{\ar{حسنًا}} closes the choice, and \textbf{\ar{شكرًا}} acknowledges it. The passage is connected by meaning before it is connected by grammar.

The first and last lines share \textbf{\ar{س}-\ar{ل}-\ar{م}}. Arabic opens the encounter with peace and closes it with safety, so the oldest root in the book gives the whole reading a frame.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the whole encounter aloud, once, without stopping
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which line calls the learner by name? (\textbf{\ar{مرحبًا} \ar{يا} \ar{سامي}.})

Which drink is declined, and which is accepted? (\textbf{\ar{حليب}: \ar{لا}. \ar{شاي}: \ar{نعم}.})

Which line closes the encounter? (\textbf{\ar{مع} \ar{السلامة}.})
\end{tcolorbox}
